hook.question: A delivery app logs its orders hour by hour. How do you find the busiest 3-hour stretch of the day without adding up every stretch from scratch?
paragraphs: You have 24 numbers, one per hour: 4, 7, 3, 9, 12, 8, 5, and so on. The slow way adds up every possible stretch separately: 22 stretches, 3 numbers each, 66 additions in total.
Now look at two neighbouring stretches, hours 3 to 5 and hours 4 to 6. They share two of their three hours. Why add those two again?
hook.aha: Don't rebuild the stretch, move it. When it slides one hour, subtract the hour that left and add the hour that arrived. That costs the same two steps whether the stretch is 3 hours long or 3,000.

metaphor: Sit by a train window and you only see one slice of the landscape. As the train rolls on, one new tree appears at the front edge and one old tree slips off the back edge.
You never re-look at the trees in the middle. You just notice what entered and what left. A sliding window is that frame laid over an array.
mentalModel.click: Never recompute the window. When it moves, add the one that entered and subtract the one that left.

glossary.definition: The stretch of neighbouring elements you are looking at right now, from left to right.
Move the right edge forward so one more element joins the window.
Move the left edge forward so the oldest element leaves the window.
The rule your window must satisfy after every step, like 'exactly k numbers' or 'no repeated letters'.
A window whose size is given (k). It always expands once and shrinks once per step.
A window whose size changes. It expands until the rule is met or broken, then shrinks until it is fixed or as small as it can be.

mentalModel.definition: A sliding window keeps a running summary (a sum, a count, a set of letters) of a contiguous range of an array or string. Two indices, left and right, mark the edges of the range and only ever move forward. Each element enters the window once and leaves at most once, so the summary is updated at the edges instead of recomputed, and the whole pass takes O(n) time.

useWhen: The problem says contiguous, subarray or substring.
A window size is given: "of size k" or "k consecutive".
It asks for the longest or shortest stretch such that some condition holds.
Brute force would re-check overlapping ranges again and again.
notWhen: The elements don't have to be next to each other (subsequences, pairs anywhere): think hash maps or dynamic programming.
You need to compare pairs from both ends of a sorted array: that is two pointers.
Numbers can be negative and the rule is "sum at least target": shrinking no longer lowers the sum, so reach for prefix sums with a monotonic deque.

quiz.problem: Given an array of daily sales and a number k, return the largest total of any k consecutive days.
quiz.explanation: "k consecutive" means a contiguous window of fixed size. Slide it and update the total at the two edges.

quiz.problem: Given a sorted array, find two numbers anywhere in it that add up to a target.
quiz.explanation: The two numbers don't have to sit next to each other, so there is no window. Because the array is sorted, one pointer at each end can close in on the target.

quiz.problem: Count the subarrays whose sum equals k. The numbers can be negative.
quiz.explanation: With negatives, shrinking the window doesn't always lower the sum, so the window rule breaks. Running totals with a lookup of earlier totals handle it.

quiz.problem: Find the longest substring that contains at most 2 different letters.
quiz.explanation: A substring is contiguous and the rule (at most 2 different letters) can be checked as the window grows, so expand and shrink a variable window.

quiz.problem: In how many different ways can you climb n stairs if each move is 1 or 2 steps?
quiz.explanation: There is no array to slide over. Each answer is built from the answers for smaller staircases, which is dynamic programming.

pseudocode.text: for each right from 0 to n - 1:
if the window holds more than k numbers:
drop nums[left] and move left on
if the window holds exactly k numbers:
best = the better of best and the window

notes: Each element is added once by right and dropped at most once by left, so the whole pass is at most 2n small steps: O(n).
For a variable-size window, turn the "too many?" if into a while loop. Keep shrinking until the rule holds again (or, for "shortest", until the window stops being big enough).
Space depends on the summary you keep: a running sum is O(1), a set or a count of letters grows with the window or the alphabet.
left and right only move forward. If you need to move one backwards, this isn't the pattern.

examples.title: Maximum Average Subarray I
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, find the contiguous subarray of length k with the largest average, and return that average.
approach: The window has a fixed size, so its average is just its sum divided by k. Compare sums and divide once at the end.
Sum the first 4 numbers: 1 + 12 - 5 - 6 = 2. That is the best so far.
Slide right: add the new number, subtract the one that left. The sums are 51 (12, -5, -6, 50) and then 42 (-5, -6, 50, 3).
The best sum is 51, so the answer is 51 / 4 = 12.75.

examples.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
examples.problem: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target, or 0 if there is none.
approach: The size isn't given, so this is a variable window. Expand right until the sum reaches the target.
While the sum is still at least target, record the length and shrink from the left to look for a shorter one.
The window [2, 3, 1, 2] is the first that works (length 4). Shrinking and expanding finds [1, 2, 4] (length 3) and finally [4, 3] (length 2).
Numbers are positive, so shrinking always lowers the sum. That is why the loop is safe.

examples.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
examples.problem: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character.
approach: The rule is "no repeated letters", so keep a set of the letters inside the window.
Before adding s[right], shrink from the left while that letter is already in the set.
Then add it and compare the window length with the best so far.
The longest window is "abc" (length 3). "bca" and "cab" tie it, and none is longer.

conceptQuiz.question: Why is a sliding window faster than re-adding every stretch from scratch?
options: It skips the middle of the array.
Neighbouring windows overlap, so only the two edges need updating.
It splits the array in half with recursion.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Each new window shares almost all of its elements with the previous one, so you only add the element that arrived and remove the one that left.

conceptQuiz.question: A window of size 3 slides one step to the right. What changes?
options: One number leaves on the left and one arrives on the right.
Only a new number is added on the right.
The window is rebuilt starting from the left edge.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Two of the three numbers stay. The oldest leaves and the next one joins, so the size stays at 3.

conceptQuiz.question: There is a while loop inside the for loop. Why is the sliding window still O(n)?
options: The while loop only runs once in total.
The array is processed in chunks of size k.
The inner loop is skipped when the input is sorted.
left only moves forward, so across the whole run it moves at most n times.
conceptQuiz.explanation: right makes n moves and left makes at most n moves. The inner loop doesn't restart left, so the total stays about 2n.

conceptQuiz.question: For "shortest subarray with sum at least target" (positive numbers), when do you shrink?
options: After every expand, whatever the sum is.
While the sum is still at least the target.
Only when the sum is below the target.
conceptQuiz.explanation: As long as the sum still reaches the target, a shorter window might also work, so keep dropping from the left. Stop when the sum falls below the target.

conceptQuiz.question: Which of these is a poor fit for a plain sliding window?
options: Longest substring with no repeated letter.
Count subarrays that sum to k when numbers can be negative.
Shortest run of positive numbers adding up to at least 20.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Negative numbers mean that shrinking can raise the sum, so you can't tell when to expand or shrink. The other three have a rule that moves in one clear direction.

practice.title: Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length
practice.insight: The window size is fixed, so it is the same slide as the sum problem, but you keep a count of vowels instead of a sum.

practice.title: Max Consecutive Ones III
practice.insight: Don't flip anything. Just look for the longest window that contains at most k zeros.

practice.title: Fruit Into Baskets
practice.insight: It is the longest window with at most two different values, so keep a small count of each value and shrink when a third appears.

practice.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
practice.insight: A window is fine when its length minus the count of its most common letter is at most k.

practice.title: Permutation in String
practice.insight: A permutation has the same letter counts as the original, so slide a window of that exact length and compare counts.

practice.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
practice.insight: Same fixed window as the permutation problem, but record every start index where the counts match instead of stopping at the first.

practice.title: Minimum Window Substring
practice.insight: Expand until the window has every needed letter, then shrink while it still does, tracking how many letters are still missing.

practice.title: Sliding Window Maximum
practice.insight: A running sum won't give you a maximum. Keep only the indices that could still become the maximum, in order, and drop the rest.
